entries.es: Tendinopatía de la porción media del tendón de Aquiles

sources.title: Achilles Pain, Stiffness, and Muscle Power Deficits: Midportion Achilles Tendinopathy Revision - 2024
sources.population: Clinically diagnosed midportion Achilles tendinopathy; recommendation excludes presumed tendon frailty.
sources.findings: Tendon loading first-line (grade A); final frequency at least 3/week (grade E). Complete rest not indicated; activity within pain tolerance. No universally superior loading type.
sources.limitations: Frequency is an expert recommendation, not proof of an optimal numeric threshold. Insertional pathology outside scope. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Heavy Slow Resistance Versus Eccentric Training as Treatment for Achilles Tendinopathy: A Randomized Controlled Trial.
sources.population: Recreational athletes with chronic >3-month unilateral midportion Achilles tendinopathy, age eligibility 18–60; insertional disease excluded.
sources.findings: VISA-A/pain improved in both at 12 and 52 weeks, no between-group superiority. HSR adherence 92% versus 78%.
sources.limitations: Small sample, no untreated comparator; no inference that eccentric loading caused rupture. Full-ROM protocol not insertional evidence. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Continued sports activity, using a pain-monitoring model, during rehabilitation in patients with Achilles tendinopathy: a randomized controlled study.
sources.population: Achilles tendinopathy patients receiving progressive rehabilitation; exact anatomical eligibility not verified from abstract.
sources.findings: No significant difference in rate of improvement; both improved VISA-A/pain through12 months. Does not establish unrestricted sport safety.
sources.limitations: Small monitored sample; full loading/harms methods not retrieved. Do not export a numeric pain threshold. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

entries.es: Tendinopatía insercional del tendón de Aquiles

sources.title: Effectiveness of reducing tendon compression in the rehabilitation of insertional Achilles tendinopathy: a randomised clinical trial.
sources.population: Sport-active adults18–60 with insertional symptoms >3 months and <3 years, VISA-A<80, running-based sport≥2/week; ultrasound-confirmed.
sources.findings: VISA-A difference favored low compression:12.9 (95%CI6.2–19.6) at12 weeks;10.4 (3.7–17.1) at24 weeks. Cannot isolate range, heel lifts or omitted stretching.
sources.limitations: Small athletic sample; low-compression package not proof that all dorsiflexion causes injury. Supplemental brochure has stage-specific doses; symptom response does not prove tissue healing. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Comparative short-term effectiveness of non-surgical treatments for insertional Achilles tendinopathy: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
sources.population: Trials diagnosed insertional Achilles tendinopathy, not midportion-only disease.
sources.findings: Eccentric exercise plus soft-tissue therapy ranked favorably for short-term pain, but confidence low/verylow; authors could not recommend a best treatment.
sources.limitations: Small heterogeneous studies; ranking does not validate a precise exercise or universal contraindication. Predates2025 compression RCT. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

entries.en: Plantar heel pain compatible with plantar fasciitis
entries.es: Dolor plantar del talón compatible con fascitis plantar

sources.title: Heel Pain - Plantar Fasciitis: Revision 2023.
sources.population: Clinically compatible plantar fasciitis/nonarthritic heel pain.
sources.findings: Recommends fascia-specific and gastrocnemius/soleus stretching; foot/ankle resistance training (gradeB); best dose/strength type unresolved.
sources.limitations: Not diagnosis of every heel pain; combined evidence cannot isolate optimal exercise or establish blanket activity prohibitions. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: A randomized controlled trial with 12-month follow-up.
sources.population: Adults with ultrasound-verified plantar fasciitis and heel pain≥3 months.
sources.findings: FFI favored strength at3 months by29 points (95%CI6–52); no between-group difference at1,6,12 months.
sources.limitations: Small sample/attrition; short-term improvement not durable superiority. Toe-extension setup conflicts with independent first-MTP range limits. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Management of plantar heel pain: a best practice guide informed by a systematic review, expert clinical reasoning and patient values.
sources.population: People with plantar heel pain; different sources inform different guide elements.
sources.findings: Core guide favored fascia stretching, taping, education; break prolonged static loading and adjust aggravating activity.
sources.limitations: Only abstract/indexed selected full-text sections inspected here; expert-reasoning advice not trial proof of a specific harmful activity dose. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Ankle Stability and Movement Coordination Impairments: Lateral Ankle Ligament Sprains Revision 2021.
sources.population: Acute/postacute lateral sprains and chronic ankle instability, separately classified.
sources.findings: Acute: progressive weight bearing with external support, structured protected ROM/neuromuscular/balance rehab; severe injury may need up to10 daysimmobilisation. CAI: proprioceptive/neuromuscular exercise; supports alone insufficient for postural stability.
sources.limitations: Severity/healing/impairment assessment required; no self-prescribed acute fracture or severe-sprain protocol. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Effect of accelerated rehabilitation on function after ankle sprain: randomised controlled trial.
sources.population: Assessed acute gradeI/II ankle sprain.
sources.findings: LEFS favored early exercise atweeks1,2 (adjusted5.28,4.92); no other pain/swelling differences.
sources.limitations: Cannot transfer to gradeIII, fracture or undifferentiated injury; full exercise dosing inaccessible. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Effect of early supervised physiotherapy on recovery from acute ankle sprain: randomised controlled trial.
sources.population: Age≥16 with simple gradeI/II sprain; injuries requiring immobilisation excluded.
sources.findings: Excellent3-month FAOS recovery43%versus37%; difference6%(95%CI−3 to15); no clinically important functional improvement through6 months.
sources.limitations: No proof exercise is harmful/unnecessary for all injuries; the particular added supervised program did not improve major outcome. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Exercise-based rehabilitation reduces reinjury following acute lateral ankle sprain: A systematic review update with meta-analysis.
sources.population: Adults after acute ankle sprain; reported sample2182 abstract versus2184 body.
sources.findings: Abstract reinjury OR0.60(95%CI0.36–0.99); sensitivity excluding high-risk exercise content lost significance; patient/clinical outcomes inconsistent.
sources.limitations: Optimal content/dose unknown; abstract/body count discrepancy retained. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Ankle Stability and Movement Coordination Impairments: Lateral Ankle Ligament Sprains Revision 2021.
sources.population: Acute/postacute lateral sprains and chronic ankle instability, separately classified.
sources.findings: Acute: progressive weight bearing with external support, structured protected ROM/neuromuscular/balance rehab; severe injury may need up to10 daysimmobilisation. CAI: proprioceptive/neuromuscular exercise; supports alone insufficient for postural stability.
sources.limitations: Severity/healing/impairment assessment required; no self-prescribed acute fracture or severe-sprain protocol. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Balance- and Strength-Training Protocols to Improve Chronic Ankle Instability Deficits, Part I: Assessing Clinical Outcome Measures.
sources.population: Young adults with CAI, questionnaire score≥11.
sources.findings: Both active arms improved balance/strength/side-hop at6 weeks; strength also improved eccentric eversion.
sources.limitations: Small sample; whole-program effects cannot be assigned to isolated stance/band exercise. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Strength-training protocols to improve deficits in participants with chronic ankle instability: a randomized controlled trial.
sources.population: Mostly college-age CAI defined with functional-instability questionnaire.
sources.findings: Strength/perceived instability improved; neither active program improved Y-Balance/crossover-hop.
sources.limitations: Not equivalent to all-components2018 protocol; strength gain not restoration of all function. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: A systematic review and meta-analysis of balance training in patients with chronic ankle instability.
sources.population: CAI trial mean ages~16–34 in Table1, despite abstract referring to older patients.
sources.findings: Balance versus blank improved CAIT MD3.95(95%CI3.26–4.64); selected SEBT directions improved. Versus strength, scale benefits but dynamic-stability differences not established.
sources.limitations: Small heterogeneous trials and limited blinding; not evidence for a universal balance dose. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Exercise for posterior tibial tendon dysfunction: a systematic review of randomised clinical trials and clinical guidelines.
sources.population: Mostly women in their 50 s with stage I/II posterior tibial dysfunction/tendinopathy.
sources.findings: Possible added eccentric benefit, but sparse evidence and poor dose reporting. The moderate home program in Houck showed minimal additional benefit.
sources.limitations: Only three small early-stage trials, sparse exercise reporting and multimodal care. Table 3 is an indirect extraction of primary protocols, whose exact apparatus was not independently verified. No generalisation to advanced rigid deformity. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Nonsurgical management of posterior tibial tendon dysfunction with orthoses and resistive exercise: a randomized controlled trial.
sources.population: Adults with stage I/II posterior tibial tendinopathy.
sources.findings: FFI improved in all groups; the eccentric group improved most. Pain after the five-minute walk improved across groups.
sources.limitations: Small early-stage trial with orthoses/stretching in every arm and no untreated comparator. Full primary exercise protocol and harms not retrieved; review-extracted details must remain attributed to the review. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Randomized Controlled Trial Comparing Orthosis Augmented by Either Stretching or Stretching and Strengthening for Stage II Tibialis Posterior Tendon Dysfunction.
sources.population: Middle-aged adults with stage II dysfunction managed with an orthosis.
sources.findings: Both groups improved pain/function; between-group differences were minimal. Deep posterior-compartment isometric strength did not differ.
sources.limitations: Moderate home strengthening added little to orthosis/stretching. Full primary methods/harms unavailable; trial cannot establish a universally ineffective or harmful exercise. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: The ESSKA-AFAS international consensus statement on peroneal tendon pathologies.
sources.population: Peroneal tendon pathologies; distinguish tendinopathy from tear, rupture and dislocation.
sources.findings: Consensus supports conservative care, painless weight bearing followed by ROM and tendon loading as appropriate. Dose is unvalidated. Conservative references include mixed-tendon PRP and luxation/subluxation reports, not an isolated-tendinopathy exercise RCT.
sources.limitations: Consensus rests on sparse evidence, including mixed-tendon and subluxation reports. It does not establish an isolated-tendinopathy exercise dose. Postoperative repair limits are a separate population. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Novel use of a manual therapy technique and management of a patient with peroneal tendinopathy: a case report.
sources.population: A 50-year-old woman with chronic lateral ankle symptoms consistent with peroneal tendinopathy.
sources.findings: Pain, function, heel raises and balance improved over eight visits; patient returned to work and recreational exercise.
sources.limitations: Single case with multiple treatments and no comparator; exact home program and harms unavailable. Improvement cannot be attributed to strengthening alone. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Role of Peroneal Tenography in Chronic Peroneal Disorders: A Service Evaluation.
sources.population: Adults with mixed chronic peroneal disorders, including tendinosis and tears; median age 50.
sources.findings: Fifteen of 27 reported adequate pain relief after tenography. This is not an exercise efficacy estimate.
sources.limitations: Retrospective mixed-pathology series selected for diagnostic/interventional care. Band strengthening dose and isolated effect are unknown; tenography benefit is not exercise evidence. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: The treatment of medial tibial stress syndrome in athletes; a randomized clinical trial.
sources.population: Athletes older than 16 with symptoms longer than three weeks and diffuse posteromedial tenderness of at least 5 cm. Suspected stress fracture/compartment syndrome was excluded.
sources.findings: Mean completion time was 105.2, 117.6 and 102.1 days respectively, with no significant between-group difference or satisfaction benefit.
sources.limitations: No rest/no-treatment comparator and substantial noncompletion. Trial-screened MTSS pain values cannot be exported to suspected fracture or every severity. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Effects of Integrating Lower-Leg Exercises Into a Multimodal Therapeutic Approach on Medial Tibial Stress Syndrome Management Among Recreational Runners: A Randomized Controlled Study.
sources.population: Recreational runners with diagnosed MTSS; mean age 23.9, 40% women.
sources.findings: No added improvement in pain or MTSS severity at six/twelve weeks. Quality-of-life and foot-posture measures improved with added exercise.
sources.limitations: Small multimodal trial with no isolated exercise-component effect. Posture/QoL improvement does not establish pain reduction or prevention of bone stress injury. Exercise frequency was not clear in inspected methods. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Load-induced medial leg pain in runners: A systematic review of non-invasive treatment approaches.
sources.population: Runners with MTSS/load-induced medial leg pain.
sources.findings: No clearly superior treatment. Exercise additions did not outperform comparators; short-term orthosis benefit was not maintained.
sources.limitations: Only three heterogeneous trials; abstract/selected introduction access cannot establish a full protocol. This is treatment evidence, separate from prevention studies. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

entries.es: Lesión ósea por estrés de la extremidad inferior

sources.title: International Delphi consensus on bone stress injuries in athletes.
sources.population: Athletes with bone stress injury; site, severity and sport demands affect management.
sources.findings: High-risk consensus sites included superior femoral-neck cortex, anterior tibia, navicular and fifth-metatarsal base. Management/return varies by site, severity, pain-free function and loading tests.
sources.limitations: Expert consensus rather than trial evidence. Full recommendation tables not retrieved; no universal rehabilitation dose or permission to load an unassessed fracture follows. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Criteria and Guidelines for Returning to Running Following a Tibial Bone Stress Injury: A Scoping Review.
sources.population: Return to running after tibial BSI; low-risk posteromedial injury differs from high-risk anterior cortex.
sources.findings: Consider pain-free walking, tenderness, strength/loading capacity and radiological healing for high-risk injury. Tenderness criteria conflict; the 10% progression rule is not universally supported.
sources.limitations: Most sources are low-level evidence; tenderness criteria conflict. Later-stage resistance/plyometric suggestions often rely on other populations and do not establish acute-fracture safety. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Correlation of MRI grading of bone stress injuries with clinical risk factors and return to play: a 5-year prospective study in collegiate track and field athletes.
sources.population: Collegiate track/cross-country athletes under clinical care.
sources.findings: Grades 3–4 returned in 23.6 ± 2.4 weeks versus 13.1 ± 2.0 for grades 1–2. Higher MRI grade and lower BMD predicted longer recovery.
sources.limitations: Prognostic associations and group averages under clinical care are not individual clearance dates or exercise-dose trials. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

entries.es: Artrosis de la primera articulación metatarsofalángica

sources.title: Non-surgical interventions for treating osteoarthritis of the big toe joint.
sources.population: First-MTP/big-toe OA; a small functional hallux-limitus trial is indirect.
sources.findings: Moderate-certainty evidence of no clinically important benefit from arch-contouring orthoses or shoe-stiffening inserts versus sham; other treatments/exercise remain uncertain.
sources.limitations: Few trials and limited exercise evidence; functional hallux-limitus findings may be indirect for radiographic OA. Partial full-review inspection conservatively classified abstract-only. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Effectiveness of Foot Orthoses Versus Rocker-Sole Footwear for First Metatarsophalangeal Joint Osteoarthritis: Randomized Trial.
sources.population: Symptomatic first-MTP OA; recurrent fallers excluded.
sources.findings: FHSQ difference 2.05 (95% CI −3.61 to 7.71), with similar improvement. Shoes had lower adherence and more adverse events (39% versus 16%; RR 2.47, 95% CI 1.12–5.44). See mtp-erratum for the separately corrected FFI endpoint.
sources.limitations: Active comparison without sham cannot isolate efficacy. Device exclusions do not establish exercise contraindications. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Effect of foot orthoses vs sham insoles on first metatarsophalangeal joint osteoarthritis symptoms: a randomized controlled trial.
sources.population: Adults at least 45 with symptomatic radiographic first-MTP OA.
sources.findings: No pain superiority: difference −0.3 NRS (95% CI −1.2 to 0.6); no secondary-outcome superiority.
sources.limitations: No superiority of contoured orthoses over sham; not a test of motion restrictions or exercise. Entire primary article inspection not completed. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: The effect of sesamoid mobilization, flexor hallucis strengthening, and gait training on reducing pain and restoring function in individuals with hallux limitus: a clinical trial.
sources.population: Functional hallux limitus with pain, motion loss and weakness; not necessarily radiographic OA.
sources.findings: The added bundle improved ROM, flexor strength and pain after 12 visits (P<.001); isolated exercise effect and durability remain unknown.
sources.limitations: Small functional hallux-limitus multimodal trial, indirect for radiographic OA. Full exact exercise methods and harms unavailable; no isolated strengthening effect. Research candidate only; no clinical release.

sources.title: Errata.
sources.population: Linked to the 2016 Menz first-MTP orthoses/footwear trial.
sources.findings: Corrects 12-week Foot Function Index scores in Table 2; corrected scores still show no between-group difference. The notice does not change the FHSQ or adverse-event endpoints.
sources.limitations: Correction is not independent replication or an exercise trial.

sources.title: Strong, steady and straight: UK consensus statement on physical activity and exercise for osteoporosis
sources.population: People with osteoporosis, stratified by vertebral/multiple low-trauma fractures, fall history and frailty.
sources.findings: Recommends resistance, impact, balance and spinal-extensor approaches. Most spine-sparing and fracture-specific modifications are consensus rather than directly proven risk thresholds.
sources.limitations: No universal weight limit or ban on all twisting/lifting. Fracture-specific impact advice explicitly precautionary.

sources.title: High-Intensity Resistance and Impact Training Improves Bone Mineral Density and Physical Function in Postmenopausal Women With Osteopenia and Osteoporosis: The LIFTMOR Randomized Controlled Trial
sources.population: Otherwise healthy postmenopausal women >58 years, hip/spine T-score <−1.0; screened for conditions/drugs influencing bone/function. Recent fracture/back pain excluded.
sources.findings: At 8 months LS BMD change 2.9±2.8% vs −1.2±2.8% (p<0.001); FN 0.3±2.6% vs −1.9±2.6% (p=0.004). These are changes±SD, not confidence intervals; no fracture-reduction effect established.
sources.limitations: Cannot transfer >80–85%1RM lifting or drop landings to unsupervised app users, acute/recent fractures or excluded comorbidity groups.

sources.title: High-Intensity Resistance and Impact Training Improves Bone Mineral Density and Physical Function in Postmenopausal Women With Osteopenia and Osteoporosis: The LIFTMOR Randomized Controlled Trial [Published Erratum]
sources.population: Original LIFTMOR cohort.
sources.findings: Table2 headings changed from % change to Change (absolute values); HiRIT calcium intake change corrected to −10±282 instead of +10±282.
sources.limitations: Correction supplies no new exercise efficacy or clearance.

sources.title: Exercise for fracture prevention - evidence and consensus-based practice guideline of the osteology umbrella association (DVO)
sources.population: Community-dwelling men/postmenopausal women≥45, varying BMD, fractures and fall risk; institutionalized/younger populations outside scope.
sources.findings: Supports bone strength/fall prevention exercise; optimal single fracture-prevention protocol remains unknown.
sources.limitations: Risk strata differ: restrictions on dynamic high back-extension/flexion loading coexist with supervised low-stimulus trunk exercise in fracture/fall-risk cohorts. No diagnosis-only ban on all trunk movement.

sources.title: Postmenopausal spinal osteoporosis: flexion versus extension exercises
sources.population: 59 women age49–60 with postmenopausal spinal osteoporosis and back pain.
sources.findings: Additional radiographic wedging/compression: extension16%, flexion89%, combined53%, noexercise67%. Flexion versus extension p<0.001; no adjusted risk or confidence interval.
sources.limitations: No universal safe angle/load or causal claim about every bend follows.

sources.title: 2022 American College of Rheumatology (ACR) Guideline for Exercise, Rehabilitation, Diet, and Additional Integrative Interventions for Rheumatoid Arthritis
sources.population: RA adults, supplementary to DMARD treatment; surgical interventions outside scope.
sources.findings: Overall exercise strong recommendation,moderate certainty; resistance conditional,very-low certainty. Dose/type not formally fixed.
sources.limitations: Joint damage,deformity,activity,comorbidity and capabilities require tailoring; no blanket joint-loading exclusion.

sources.title: Is a long-term high-intensity exercise program effective and safe in patients with rheumatoid arthritis? Results of a randomized controlled trial
sources.population: RA adults; baseline large-joint damage subgroup highlighted; details not established from abstract.
sources.findings: MACTAR change difference year2 3.1 (95%CI0.7–5.5); HAQ −0.09 (−0.18 to−0.01). Overall median large-joint damage not increased; considerable baseline-damage group may progress more.
sources.limitations: Cannot translate subgroup signal into all-RA weight cap; no fulltext protocol.

sources.title: High-intensity interval training improves cardiovascular and physical health in patients with rheumatoid arthritis: a multicentre randomised controlled trial
sources.population: RA>1year,stable antirheumatic medication3months,DAS28<5.1; prescreened rheumatologist/CPET, cardiovascular and participation-limiting comorbidity excluded.
sources.findings: VO2max difference3.71mL/kg/min (95%CI2.16–5.25). Pain −4.0 (−13.07 to5.06),DAS28 −0.25 (−0.60 to0.10): no significant differences. Fitness benefit is not proof of anti-inflammatory efficacy.
sources.limitations: Not transferable to severe/unstable RA, all damaged joints, or unscreened HIIT.

sources.title: EULAR recommendations for physical activity in people with inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis: 2025 update
sources.population: Inflammatory arthritis including RA/SpA and hip/knee OA; condition-specific adaptation still needed.
sources.findings: Recommends assessment, individualized adaptation, competent delivery and explicit FITT-volume-progression; no single optimal execution.
sources.limitations: The24-hour rule is an example used in some studies;48–72hour soreness can occur. Neither is a validated universal stop threshold.

sources.title: Efficacy of High Intensity Exercise on Disease Activity and Cardiovascular Risk in Active Axial Spondyloarthritis: A Randomized Controlled Pilot Study
sources.population: ASAS axSpA,18–70,BASDAI≥3.5,stable TNF-inhibitor use3months,no regular endurance/strength>1h/week in prior year. No established CVD/limiting comorbidity.
sources.findings: ASDAS mean difference−0.7 (95%CI−1.4 to0.1),crosses null; BASDAI−2.0 (−3.6 to−0.4);BASFI−1.4 (−2.6 to−0.3);VO2peak+3.7 (2.1–5.2). Primary result uncertainty must not be hidden by secondary benefits.
sources.limitations: Not an advanced ankylosis/fracture or postoperative trial; absence of observed flare is not universal safety.

sources.title: High intensity exercise for 3 months reduces disease activity in axial spondyloarthritis (axSpA): a multicentre randomised trial of 100 patients
sources.population: AxSpA adults; detailed inclusion/stage distribution not extracted from abstract.
sources.findings: At3months ASDAS treatment effect−0.6 (95%CI−0.8 to−0.3);BASDAI−1.2 (−1.8 to−0.7). Function,inflammation and cardiovascular health also improved.
sources.limitations: Abstract supports benefit but not an exact app protocol.

sources.title: Korean College of Rheumatology treatment recommendations for patients with axial spondyloarthritis: 2026 update
sources.population: Adults with axSpA in Korean care context.
sources.findings: Strong recommendation regular exercise;low certainty disease activity/function from mostly unblinded studies. Spinal mobility evidence more robust; no single optimal routine.
sources.limitations: No universal range/impact/load thresholds or postoperative execution.

sources.title: EULAR recommendations for physical activity in people with inflammatory arthritis and osteoarthritis: 2025 update
sources.population: Inflammatory arthritis including RA/SpA and hip/knee OA; condition-specific adaptation still needed.
sources.findings: Recommends assessment, individualized adaptation, competent delivery and explicit FITT-volume-progression; no single optimal execution.
sources.limitations: The24-hour rule is an example used in some studies;48–72hour soreness can occur. Neither is a validated universal stop threshold.

sources.title: Resistance exercise improves muscle strength, health status and pain intensity in fibromyalgia—a randomized controlled trial
sources.population: Women20–65 meeting ACR1990 criteria;actual22–64,variable chronic symptom duration; competing severe pain/comorbidity excluded.
sources.findings: Knee-extension force between-group p=0.010,effect size0.55;FIQ p=0.038,effect size0.41;pain p=0.033,effect size0.46. No95%CI for these standardized effects in extracted table. Handgrip/SF36 group differences not significant;13–18month self-report group differences absent.
sources.limitations: Individual readiness governs progression: 42/67 participants (62.7%) reached 80% estimated 1RM. No automatic progression or universal tolerability follows.

sources.title: Effect of tai chi versus aerobic exercise for fibromyalgia: comparative effectiveness randomized controlled trial
sources.population: Age≥21,ACR1990/2010criteria;92%women,mean52;serious participation-limiting disease,inflammatory/connective-tissue disease and recent tai chi excluded.
sources.findings: 24weekFIQR combined tai-chi advantage5.5points (95%CI0.6–10.4),below borrowed8.1pointFIQclinical threshold;matched24week2×/weekcontrast16.2 (8.7–23.6). At52weeks combined difference2.7 (−2.3 to7.7),not significant. Twice-versus-once weekly advantage not significant.
sources.limitations: Tai chi is not a single stretch or strength-set substitute;exact Yang forms not fully extracted for app artwork.

sources.title: Brazilian Society of Rheumatology’s fibromyalgia treatment guidelines – part I: monitoring and non-pharmacological management
sources.population: Fibromyalgia management; evidence predominantly women with heterogeneous trials.
sources.findings: Recommends aerobic/resistance approaches;flexibility generally less effective and lacks clinically significant advantage versus aerobic for several outcomes.
sources.limitations: No condition-wide high-intensity/ROM ban and no single validated default dose.

sources.title: Short-term effectiveness of high-load compared with low-load strengthening exercise on self-reported function in patients with hypermobile shoulders: a randomised controlled trial
sources.population: Generalized or historical HSD, age 18–65, shoulder pain/instability at least 3 months; 79% women, mean age 37.8. No hEDS enrolled. Shoulder surgery within 1 year and injection within 3 months excluded.
sources.findings: At 16 weeks, WOSI adjusted between-group difference −174.5/2100 (95% CI −341.4 to −7.7), 8.3%, below the predefined minimal important difference. Most secondary outcomes inconclusive; NNT 7 (95% CI 4–620) very imprecise.
sources.limitations: Cannot generalize to all joints, hEDS, postoperative shoulders, unsupervised loading or unrestricted end range.

sources.title: A randomised controlled trial of heavy shoulder strengthening exercise in patients with hypermobility spectrum disorder or hypermobile Ehlers-Danlos syndrome and long-lasting shoulder complaints: study protocol for the Shoulder-MOBILEX study
sources.population: Planned HSD/hEDS adults with persistent shoulder complaints; actual 2022 cohort included HSD only.
sources.findings: Defines planned execution, loading and control; does not supply an efficacy estimate.
sources.limitations: Manual advice about back twisting, bent-back work and extreme positions is untested shared education; it is not causal evidence for universal HSD restrictions.

sources.title: One-year effectiveness of high-load compared with low-load strengthening exercise on self-reported function in patients with hypermobile shoulders: a secondary analysis from a randomised controlled trial
sources.population: Same HSD shoulder cohort; 86% completed one-year follow-up.
sources.findings: WOSI change: HEAVY −456.9 (95% CI −572.2 to −341.7), LIGHT −364.0 (−481.4 to −246.6); between-group difference −92.9 (−257.4 to 71.5), not significant. Clinically important improvement: 64% versus 60%.
sources.limitations: Short-term relative advantage does not establish sustained one-year superiority.

sources.title: The effect of therapeutic exercises in individuals with joint hypermobility syndrome: a systematic review and meta-analysis
sources.population: Ages 7–45, mixed Brighton/Beighton diagnoses, JHS/EDS; indirect for contemporary adult HSD.
sources.findings: Pain effect CI −2.164 to −0.357, with high heterogeneity (I² 81.799%); strength CI −0.389 to 0.495, nonsignificant. Effects were not uniform across outcomes.
sources.limitations: Does not establish a blanket HSD stretching/end-range ban or justify shoulder-to-knee transfer.
